Mugshot is a fast-paced player-versus-player investigation game where you must identify a suspect in a lineup of culprits as quickly as possible. However, the suspect sketches are drawings by artists with completely different styles!

In Mugshot, we highlight how humans perceive each other, through artists' drawings and the photos displayed in the lineup. By removing spatial and visual cues for players, Mugshot encourages them to change the way they recognize faces, even when those people are part of their close circle.

With the Pumpkin team, we defined a few user stories representing the main intentions of our game. From these user stories come many tasks, all prioritized using the MoSCow method. This list is not exhaustive but serves as a common foundation to project ourselves more calmly into the coming weeks. User stories do not have assigned persons since this workload relates to the tasks that stem from them. Each task is estimated in story points, meaning according to a complexity scale for completing the task using the Poker Planning method. In my opinion, it is relevant to use this method rather than tracking time spent compared to estimated time, which is often inaccurate given the particular schedules we have in our school context where we still juggle between project time and classes. Estimating by complexity mainly allows for debate and pointing out potential blockers, and therefore, prioritizing a task or not depending on the situation.

At the beginning of each sprint, we estimate the complexity of the tasks we wish to accomplish and check whether we are setting ourselves overly ambitious goals thanks to a collective estimation of our 'Capacity to Deliver' based on past sprints. We organize our time and workload more flexibly while keeping project milestones as major markers of project progress.
We have established a weekly meeting to report on progress, discuss potential blockers, and celebrate successes.

In parallel, we intend to set up written dailies while we still have classes, to keep each other informed and signal when we have a dependency/need from someone on the team. In the long term, when we are fully dedicated to the projects, the goal is to switch to physical 15-minute dailies with controlled speaking time.

We do not hold sprint reviews or retrospectives (mainly due to lack of time), but we regularly share our progress in our communication channels through short videos and test with each other every week. We sometimes also have our prototypes tested by people outside the team, even if it's not an official or structured playtest, to gather opinions different from ours, as we sometimes have a vision too anchored in the project.

Raccoon Rampage is a project created as part of the CNAM-ENJMIN school's Ateliers Nano 2025, where a team of 9 game design students from each discipline creates a game based on a defined genre (Racing) and theme (Harmony).

Beans & Trashy, a duo of mischievous raccoons, joyfully discover an abandoned campsite. Armed with a dented supermarket cart, they speed through this litter-strewn forest to collect as many forgotten treasures as possible!

The game is played as a duet on one computer keyboard, although it is possible to play solo if you want to test the game alone before playing it with your friends. Cross the campsite, national park, and dump as quickly as possible, while picking up various items along the way. But beware: their effects remain to be discovered.
